headline: “Oh, shut up.” Maine’s Senate debate turns playground.
summary: A protester shouted over Thursday night's Maine Senate debate. Sen. Susan Collins said he was obviously one of Troy Jackson's supporters. "Oh, shut up," Jackson shot back. "I don't even know that kid." The race is one of a handful that will decide the Senate majority. Axios says the two sounded like children on a playground.

cover_question.q: Can you say that in a debate?

cover_answer: He did. Nobody could stop him. Maine's voters are the judge.
table_question: Is there ever a time to tell someone to shut up?

5-7.script: Two people in Maine both want the same job, and they argued about it on TV. Someone in the crowd shouted, and one of them said "Oh, shut up," the thing you're not allowed to say at the table. It's like two kids both grabbing one swing. The grown-ups in Maine will pick who gets the job, by voting.
5-7.why: The table rule they already police, and one swing for two kids.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and "shut up" is a rule they already police at home. The script gives them the one rude line and two people wanting one swing, then hands the pick to the grown-ups. Expect "does he get a time-out?" No. The voters decide instead, which is the grown-up version.

8-12.script: The two people running for Maine's Senate seat debated on Thursday. A protester started yelling. Senator Susan Collins said he was obviously one of Troy Jackson's supporters, and Jackson shot back, "Oh, shut up." A debate has no referee. The voters are, and the race is a toss-up.
8-12.why: Heckler, jab, snap. No referee is the mechanism; the voters are.
8-12.why_long: This age is testing whether adults follow the rules they set, and a candidate saying "shut up" on TV is exactly the breach they notice. The script runs the chain: a heckler, a jab, a snap. The missing referee is the mechanism, and the voters fill the job. Expect "so who wins?" Nobody knows; the race is rated a toss-up.

13-17.script: Does "shut up" cost a candidate votes, or win them? Troy Jackson said it to Senator Susan Collins on Thursday after she pinned a heckler on him, in a race that could decide the Senate. Second: asked for a time she stopped Trump and it changed the outcome, Collins named one. The moderator said it didn't.
13-17.why: Rudeness as a tactic, and a record that didn't hold up.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two things at once: the line was rude, and it may have worked. The script asks that first, then hands them Collins's Hegseth answer and the moderator's verdict that it changed nothing. Expect "would you have said it?" Answer honestly, then ask what they would have done.

5-7.q: Isn't shut up a bad word?
5-7.a: It's a rude one. A grown-up said it on TV and now everyone is talking about it, which is what happens.

8-12.q: Why did he tell her to shut up?
8-12.a: A protester yelled. She pinned him on Jackson, who snapped.

8-12.q: Does he get in trouble for it?
8-12.a: No penalty. The voters decide, and the race is a toss-up.

13-17.q: Can you say that in a debate?
13-17.a: He did. No rule stopped him. The voters judge it.
She pinned the heckler on him first. Then he snapped.
